title: Temperance
hook: enough, not too much: joy in good things rightly used

segments.voice: Yesterday, fortitude: Esther fasting first, then walking through the door. Your line was steady courage. Did you do the brave small thing? Day one thousand two hundred.

Honey. Proverbs has advice about it, and it's surprisingly practical: "Hast thou found honey? eat so much as is sufficient for thee, lest thou be filled therewith, and vomit it." No lecture about sugar. No claim that honey is bad. In fact the verse assumes you'll find some, and eat some. It just knows the moment when the next spoonful turns sweet into sick. Anyone who has finished a whole bag of something at midnight knows that moment too. Today, the last of the four cardinal virtues, the one that knows where that line is. Temperance.

Start with what temperance is not. It isn't a suspicion of good things. The Bible names plenty of them. A psalm thanks God for "wine that maketh glad the heart of man," and bread that strengthens the heart. Ecclesiastes says that to eat and drink and enjoy the good of your work "is the gift of God." And the first letter to Timothy says it outright: "every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving." So temperance starts with yes. Good food, good drink, rest, screens, shopping, work: gifts. Temperance is the skill of enjoying them at the right measure, so they stay gifts and don't become masters. Paul lists it among the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians: love, joy, peace, and on through the list, ending with "meekness, temperance: against such there is no law." The Greek word there is enkrateia, self-mastery, being in charge of your own appetite instead of the other way around. The Book of Wisdom's list of four uses a different Greek word, sophrosyne, soundness of mind; the King James calls both temperance. And notice it's called fruit. Some Christian teachers speak of it as something that grows in a person, not a rule clamped on from outside. Churches apply it differently. Some ask members not to drink alcohol at all. Others drink in moderation and use wine at communion. Both are trying to keep good things in their place. Which explains today's line. Too much honey isn't more joy. It's less. Stopping at enough is how the joy survives.

Here's the practice: find your enough. Settle, and breathe. Think of one good thing you tend to keep going with past the point of joy: scrolling, snacking, a show that rolls into the next one, a few more emails at night. Picture the moment it's good. Then picture the moment it tips, the spoonful too many. Notice where that line sits for you. Decide, gently, that today you'll stop there. If you pray, you can give thanks for the good thing itself. The bell holds the time.
Temperance. Joy in good things at the right measure. In Paul's Greek, enkrateia: being master of your appetite, not mastered by it.
Your line: enough is joy. Today, stop one good thing at enough, and notice that it's still good when you walk away. Day one thousand two hundred.

howItsDone: Some Christians practice temperance through grace before meals, fasting seasons such as Lent, and moderation in food, drink and pleasures; some churches ask members to abstain from alcohol, while others drink in moderation and use wine at communion.

original.note: Greek: self-mastery, self-control; the word translated temperance in Galatians 5:23.

trapdoor: what you thought: temperance means giving things up.
what it means: enjoying good gifts at the right measure, so they stay gifts.
what a scholar hears: the King James says temperance for two Greek words: enkrateia, self-mastery, in Galatians 5:23, and sophrosyne, soundness of mind, in Wisdom 8:7.

notes: 'The last of the four cardinal virtues' refers to this path's order (prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance) and to the four named in Wisdom 8:7 on day 1197.
Practices around alcohol described without ranking; confirm the description is fair to churches that abstain and those that use wine at communion.
Galatians 5:23: ἐγκράτεια rendered 'temperance' in the KJV; confirm original note and pronunciation.
Psalm 104:15 bread line paraphrased ('bread which strengtheneth man's heart').

Audit pass: the cardinal virtue in Wisdom 8:7 (day 1197) is σωφροσύνη, while Galatians 5:23 has ἐγκράτεια; the script presented enkrateia as the virtue's Greek without saying so. Teach now names both and the KJV's single English word; trapdoor rewritten to match. Confirm glosses.
